papers.title: spatialMET: an open and scalable framework for spatial metabolomics analysis
papers.summary: spatialMET is a new open-source software framework designed to make spatial metabolomics data analysis more scalable and accessible. It likely provides tools for processing, integrating, and visualizing spatially resolved metabolite data from tissue samples. The framework aims to standardize workflows so researchers can more easily extract biological insights from complex spatial metabolomic datasets.
papers.why: This tool could directly support the spatial metabolomics component of the PhD project, offering a scalable pipeline to analyze metabolic changes tied to mitophagy/autophagy in neurons and their microenvironment, including interneurons and perineuronal nets.

papers.title: Autophagy-lysosomal pathway in neurodegeneration.
papers.summary: This paper appears to focus on the autophagy-lysosomal pathway and its role in neurodegeneration, though the abstract itself provides no detailed content beyond the title. The autophagy-lysosomal pathway is a cellular system responsible for degrading and recycling damaged organelles and proteins, including mitochondria via mitophagy. Dysfunction in this pathway is broadly implicated across neurodegenerative diseases, making it a foundational topic for understanding neuronal health and disease.
papers.why: Understanding the autophagy-lysosomal pathway in neurodegeneration is directly relevant to studying mitophagy and autophagy dysfunction in neurons, providing mechanistic context that could inform interpretation of spatial transcriptomic and metabolomic changes in interneurons and perineuronal nets.

papers.title: Integrated Spatial Metabolomics and Proteomics from the Same Tissue Section Using a Conductive ITO-PET Slide
papers.summary: This paper presents a method to perform both spatial metabolomics and spatial proteomics on the exact same tissue section using a specialized conductive ITO-PET slide. This approach avoids the need for adjacent tissue sections, which normally introduces alignment errors and loss of molecular correlation. By combining both data types from one section, researchers can more precisely map how metabolites and proteins co-localize within the same tissue architecture.
papers.why: This technical advance in multimodal spatial metabolomics and proteomics from a single tissue section could directly improve the precision of mapping mitophagy-related protein and metabolite changes within specific neuronal populations like interneurons and their perineuronal nets.

papers.title: Revealing Hidden Variables in DESI-Based Spatial Metabolomics: Solvent Composition and Tissue Type as Critical Drivers.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how the choice of solvent and the type of tissue being analyzed can strongly influence results in DESI mass spectrometry-based spatial metabolomics. The authors treat these factors as 'hidden variables' that are often overlooked but can significantly skew metabolite detection and interpretation. Their findings suggest that careful standardization of solvent composition and tissue-specific considerations are essential for reliable and reproducible spatial metabolomics data.
papers.why: Since spatial metabolomics is a key technique for studying neuronal and perineuronal net biochemistry in this PhD project, understanding these critical technical confounders in DESI-based methods is essential for generating trustworthy, reproducible metabolomic maps of brain tissue.

papers.title: Exercise-induced intercellular mitochondrial transfer: Redox signaling as a candidate regulatory mechanism.
papers.summary: This paper proposes that intercellular mitochondrial transfer between cells can be triggered by exercise, potentially as a way to share healthy mitochondria or offload damaged ones. It suggests that redox signaling, meaning changes in reactive oxygen species and cellular oxidation states, may act as the regulatory trigger for this transfer process. The abstract frames this as a candidate mechanism rather than a proven pathway, indicating the field is still building evidence for how and why mitochondria move between cells during physical activity.
papers.why: Although focused on exercise physiology rather than brain tissue, this work touches on mitochondrial quality control and intercellular signaling mechanisms that are conceptually relevant to understanding mitophagy regulation and redox stress responses in neurons.

papers.title: Mitophagy as an active regulator of cardiac metabolic reprogramming.
papers.summary: This paper looks at mitophagy, the process cells use to clear damaged mitochondria, as a driver of metabolic changes in the heart rather than just a cleanup mechanism. It likely explores how selectively removing mitochondria reshapes energy production pathways in cardiac tissue under stress or disease conditions. The abstract suggests mitophagy actively steers metabolic reprogramming, implying a regulatory rather than passive role.
